intro.en: Vaccines tested in the paediatric practical exam: types and routes, dose rules, cold chain, individual vaccines, and the national and IAP schedules.

items.summary: A chart that groups vaccines by how they are made, with example products and the route used for each group.

blocks.title: How to read the chart
blocks.text: Match the making method on the left with its example vaccines, then read the route on the right. Examiners often ask for one example of each method with the correct route.

head: Made by
Example vaccines
Route given
rows: Measles, MMR, chickenpox, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis vaccines
Cholera, plague and whole cell pertussis vaccines
Hepatitis A, rabies and inactivated polio vaccines
Hepatitis B, acellular pertussis, influenza, HPV and anthrax vaccines
Plain polysaccharide, only after 2 years of age
23 valent pneumococcal, meningococcal and typhoid vaccines
13 valent pneumococcal, Hib and typhoid conjugate vaccines

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Plain polysaccharide vaccines protect only children above 2 years of age.
Conjugate vaccines join the polysaccharide to a protein so that infants respond as well.
BCG is the only vaccine here given into the skin, and oral polio with rotavirus are the only ones swallowed.

viva.q: Give one example each of a live and a killed vaccine with its route.
viva.a: BCG is a live bacterial vaccine given intradermally, while hepatitis B is a subunit vaccine given into muscle.

viva.q: Which vaccines need no injection?
viva.a: Oral polio and rotavirus vaccines are swallowed, so no needle is used.

viva.q: Why are some polysaccharide vaccines joined to a protein?
viva.a: Joining, called conjugation, makes them work in infants, while plain polysaccharide vaccines work only after 2 years.

items.summary: Practical rules on dose volumes, routes, sites, spacing, storage, and when vaccination must wait.

blocks.title: Dose volumes
bullets: Almost all vaccines use a single dose volume of 0.5 mL.
BCG and fractional inactivated polio vaccine use the smaller volume of 0.1 mL.
The book places hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccines after 19 years, with rabies vaccine, in a 1 mL group.
Oral polio vaccine is given as two drops, and oral rotavirus vaccine as 2 or 3 mL.

blocks.title: Routes and sites
bullets: A vaccine meant for under the skin may be placed into muscle with no harm.
The reverse is unsafe: intramuscular vaccines must not go under the skin, since aluminium salt mixes irritate the tissue and weak blood flow there weakens protection.
Never inject into the buttock, where the sciatic nerve is at risk and rabies and hepatitis B vaccines protect less well.
Inject the front and outer thigh in newborns and infants, and the deltoid of the arm in older children.
When several vaccines fall due together, place each at a separate body site, and never mix vaccines in one syringe.

blocks.title: Timing, storage and spacing
bullets: Keep vaccines between 2 deg C and 8 deg C at all times.
Only live vaccines such as oral polio, BCG and MMR may rest in the freezer compartment.
Never freeze diphtheria, tetanus, hepatitis and Hib vaccines or their diluents.
Aluminium salt is the adjuvant used most often to strengthen the response.
Two live vaccines may be given together, but if given apart keep 4 weeks between them, except for oral polio with MMR.
Two or more killed vaccines may be given together or at any gap, except cholera with yellow fever.
Reconstitute live vaccines with sterile water, except BCG which needs normal saline.
BCG works mainly through a cell based immune response.

blocks.title: When to wait, and when not to
bullets: Mild illness never blocks vaccination: a cold, loose stools, slight fever, prematurity, penicillin allergy, poor nourishment, or current antibiotic treatment are all acceptable.
Avoid every live vaccine in weak immunity, such as high dose steroid treatment or symptomatic HIV infection.
Whole cell pertussis is barred by worsening brain disease, fits after an earlier dose, or nonstop crying beyond 3 hours.
Mild fever, febrile fits and cerebral palsy do not bar whole cell pertussis.
Hepatitis B, tetanus and rabies vaccines may be given together with their matching immunoglobulin at different sites.
A newborn whose mother is hepatitis B positive or of unknown status needs both immunoglobulin and vaccine within 12 hours of birth at separate sites.
Teenagers missed earlier should still receive Tdap or Td with MMR, hepatitis B, typhoid, HPV, hepatitis A and chickenpox vaccines.

viva.q: A child has a mild cold on vaccination day. Do you postpone?
viva.a: No. Minor illness such as a cold, mild fever, diarrhoea, prematurity or antibiotic treatment is no reason to delay.

viva.q: Can two live vaccines be given on the same day?
viva.a: Yes, they may be given together, but if given apart, keep a 4 week gap, except for oral polio with MMR.

viva.q: Which vaccines must never be frozen?
viva.a: Diphtheria, tetanus, hepatitis B, hepatitis A and Hib vaccines, with their diluents, must stay between 2 and 8 deg C.

viva.q: Where do you inject an infant and an older child?
viva.a: Use the anterolateral thigh in newborns and infants and the deltoid in older children, and never the buttock.

unsure: Hepatitis A dose volume reads both as 0.5 mL and inside the 1 mL group; the 1 mL reading was kept only in this general item.
The DPT section prints storage at 4 to 8 deg C while general rules print 2 to 8 deg C; both wordings kept as printed.

items.summary: Live tuberculosis vaccine given at birth into the skin of the left upper arm.

blocks.title: Vaccine and site
bullets: BCG is a live weakened vaccine made from the Danish 1331 strain in Tamil Nadu.
Give it at birth into the skin over the left deltoid insertion with a 26 G tuberculin syringe.
The dose is 0.1 mL mixed with normal saline, and missed children may catch up until 5 years of age.
Use the mixed vaccine within 4 hours of preparation.

blocks.title: Protection and skin response
bullets: Protection reaches about 80 percent against miliary tuberculosis and meningeal disease, but only about 50 percent against lung disease.
A scar of 4 to 8 mm should appear in 8 to 12 weeks.
The Mantoux skin test turns positive after 4 weeks.
World tuberculosis day falls on 24 March.

blocks.title: When to avoid
bullets: Hold BCG in symptomatic ARC, generalised eczema, and low gamma globulin states.
Do not vaccinate during pregnancy.

blocks.title: BCG with HIV infection
bullets: Vaccinate HIV infected children on treatment who are clinically well with CD4 above 25 percent.
Vaccinate newborns when the mother HIV status is unknown, since benefit outweighs risk.
Vaccinate exposed newborns who show no signs of HIV, even when the mother takes treatment.
When early virological testing confirms HIV, wait until treatment has started and the infant is immunologically stable with CD4 above 25 percent.

viva.q: Where and how is BCG given?
viva.a: Into the skin over the left deltoid at birth, 0.1 mL with a 26 G tuberculin syringe, mixed in normal saline.

viva.q: What scar and Mantoux change do you expect?
viva.a: A 4 to 8 mm scar in 8 to 12 weeks, with Mantoux positivity from 4 weeks.

viva.q: When is BCG unsafe?
viva.a: Symptomatic ARC, generalised eczema, low gamma globulin states, pregnancy, and confirmed HIV until the infant is stable on treatment.

unsure: Book prints CD4 above 25 percent for children aged 5 years; the age wording looked garbled so it was left out.

items.summary: Polio vaccines given as drops by mouth and as a killed injection, with their schedules and vial check.

blocks.title: Oral polio vaccine
bullets: A live weakened bivalent vaccine given as two drops by mouth, starting with a zero dose at birth.
Later doses fall at 4, 6 and 14 weeks, with boosters at 18 to 24 months and at 5 years.
Give no hot fluids for half an hour afterwards, though breastfeeding may continue.
Vaccine virus leaves in the stool for up to 6 weeks, which extends cover to contacts.
Check the vial monitor and discard the vial once the inner white square darkens to the outer blue circle.

blocks.title: Inactivated polio vaccine
bullets: A killed injected vaccine that may be given alongside the oral drops, and replacing oral with injected vaccine early is ideal.
Mass drives use two fractional intradermal doses of 0.1 mL.
The strongest routine is three intramuscular doses at 6 and 14 weeks with a booster at 16 to 18 months.
Where injected vaccine is unavailable, give three bivalent oral doses and refer the child for fractional doses at 6 and 14 weeks, or at least one intramuscular dose at 14 weeks, alone or combined.

viva.q: What is the zero dose of polio vaccine?
viva.a: Oral polio drops given at birth for institutional deliveries, before the 4, 6 and 14 week doses.

viva.q: How do you read the vaccine vial monitor?
viva.a: Discard the vial when the inner white square changes colour to match the outer blue circle.

viva.q: When is fractional IPV used?
viva.a: In mass drives, as two intradermal 0.1 mL doses, while routine practice prefers intramuscular doses.

unsure: Book prints 40, 8 and 32 D antigen units against types 1 and 3, which does not align, so the figures were left out.
Book lists four still endemic countries under the mnemonic PAIN including India; this looks outdated and was left out.
Book prints bivalent types 1 and 2; the type numbering looked uncertain so only bivalent was kept.

items.summary: Combined diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine given in infancy with boosters in childhood.

blocks.title: Vaccine and schedule
bullets: Diphtheria and tetanus toxoids joined with whole cell or acellular pertussis on an aluminium salt base.
Inject 0.5 mL deep into the muscle of the outer thigh at 4, 6 and 14 weeks.
Boosters fall at 18 to 24 months and again at 5 years.
DTwP or DTaP carries 25 Lf units of diphtheria toxoid and may be used until 7 years of age.
Beyond 7 years use Td or Tdap with 2.5 Lf units of diphtheria toxoid and 5 Lf units of tetanus toxoid.
Tetanus toxoid alone holds 5 Lf units of toxoid.

blocks.title: Fever and storage
bullets: Treat fever after the shot with paracetamol 15 mg per kg.
This section prints storage at 4 to 8 deg C with no freezing.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Worsening brain disease, fits after an earlier dose, or crying beyond 3 hours bar whole cell pertussis.
Mild fever, febrile fits and cerebral palsy do not bar it.

viva.q: What is the primary schedule of DPT?
viva.a: 0.5 mL deep intramuscular at 4, 6 and 14 weeks, with boosters at 18 to 24 months and 5 years.

viva.q: What replaces DPT after 7 years of age?
viva.a: Td or Tdap with lower diphtheria content, 2.5 Lf units, and 5 Lf units of tetanus toxoid.

viva.q: How do you manage fever after DPT?
viva.a: Give paracetamol 15 mg per kg; mild fever alone never bars the next dose.

unsure: Book prints 25 Lf units of diphtheria toxoid without a clear tetanus figure for DTwP or DTaP; kept as printed.

items.summary: Live measles vaccine given under the skin at 9 months, also used after exposure.

blocks.title: Dose and preparation
bullets: A live weakened vaccine made from the Edmonston-Zagreb measles strain.
Give 0.5 mL under the skin at 9 months of age.
Mix with sterile water and use within 4 hours of mixing.

blocks.title: After exposure
bullets: Vaccinate within 72 hours of contact with a case to block the disease.

viva.q: When and how is measles vaccine given?
viva.a: 0.5 mL subcutaneous at 9 months of age, mixed in sterile water.

viva.q: How soon must you vaccinate a contact?
viva.a: Within 72 hours of exposure for post exposure protection.

viva.q: How long does the mixed vaccine keep?
viva.a: Use it within 4 hours of reconstitution, then discard the rest.

items.summary: Triple live vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella given in three childhood doses.

blocks.title: Dose and schedule
bullets: A live weakened freeze dried powder vaccine.
Mix with sterile water and use within 4 hours of mixing.
Give 0.5 mL under the skin at 9 months, a second dose at 15 months, and a third at 5 years.

blocks.title: Campaign dose
bullets: MR vaccine in national drives is given regardless of earlier shots.

viva.q: What is the MMR schedule in the book?
viva.a: 0.5 mL subcutaneous at 9 months, 15 months and 5 years.

viva.q: A child already had MMR. Do you give the campaign MR dose?
viva.a: Yes. The campaign dose is given regardless of earlier vaccination.

viva.q: How do you prepare MMR?
viva.a: Mix the freeze dried powder in sterile water and use within 4 hours.

items.summary: Recombinant subunit hepatitis B vaccine starting at birth, with cover for exposed newborns.

blocks.title: Schedule and dose
bullets: An inactivated subunit vaccine built by recombinant DNA methods.
Give at birth, 6, 10 and 14 weeks, or at 0, 1 and 6 months.
Give 0.5 mL into muscle, rising to 1 mL after 19 years of age.
Combination vaccines may justify four total doses.

blocks.title: Exposed newborn
bullets: When the mother is positive or of unknown status, give immunoglobulin plus vaccine within 12 hours of birth at different sites.

viva.q: What is the hepatitis B schedule?
viva.a: Birth, 6, 10 and 14 weeks, or 0, 1 and 6 months, 0.5 mL intramuscular.

viva.q: The mother is HBsAg positive. What does the newborn need?
viva.a: HBIG plus hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth at different sites.

viva.q: What dose does an adult over 19 years receive?
viva.a: 1 mL intramuscular, instead of the 0.5 mL childhood dose.

items.summary: Conjugate vaccine against invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b disease of early childhood.

blocks.title: Disease it prevents
bullets: This germ causes meningitis, bloodstream infection, pneumonia, middle ear infection, bone infection, septic joints, and epiglottis swelling.

blocks.title: Routine schedule
bullets: A conjugate built from Hib capsular polysaccharide.
Give 0.5 mL deep into the thigh muscle at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, with a booster at 15 to 18 months.

blocks.title: Late starters
bullets: Above 6 months of age, give two doses 4 weeks apart with a booster at 15 to 18 months.
Above 12 months of age, give two doses 4 weeks apart.
Above 15 months of age, a single dose suffices.

viva.q: What is the routine Hib schedule?
viva.a: 0.5 mL deep intramuscular at 6, 10 and 14 weeks with a booster at 15 to 18 months.

viva.q: Name three diseases Hib vaccine prevents.
viva.a: Meningitis, pneumonia and epiglottitis, besides bloodstream, ear, bone and joint infection.

viva.q: A 16 month old never had Hib. How many doses?
viva.a: One dose is enough above 15 months of age.

items.summary: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine of infancy with a plain polysaccharide form for older ages.

blocks.title: Conjugate schedule
bullets: A 13 valent pneumococcal conjugate such as Prevenar.
Give 0.5 mL under the skin or into muscle at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, with a booster at 12 to 15 months.
Preterm, very low birth weight and high risk infants are included.

blocks.title: Late starters
bullets: Above 6 months of age, give two doses 4 weeks apart with a booster at 12 to 15 months.
Above 12 months of age, give two doses 4 weeks apart.
Above 23 months of age, a single dose suffices.

blocks.title: Plain polysaccharide form
bullets: The 23 valent unconjugated vaccine such as Pneumovax is for use only after 2 years.
Give 0.5 mL as a single dose, with a second dose only for high risk groups.

viva.q: What is the infant PCV schedule?
viva.a: 0.5 mL at 6, 10 and 14 weeks with a booster at 12 to 15 months.

viva.q: When is the plain 23 valent vaccine used?
viva.a: Only after 2 years of age, as a single dose, repeated only in high risk groups.

viva.q: Which infants especially need PCV?
viva.a: Preterm, very low birth weight and high risk infants.

items.summary: Polysaccharide and conjugate typhoid vaccines with different ages and booster rules.

blocks.title: Polysaccharide form
bullets: A Vi capsular polysaccharide unconjugated vaccine.
Give 0.5 mL into muscle after 2 years of age, and repeat every 3 years.

blocks.title: Conjugate form
bullets: A single conjugate dose is advised from 6 months onward and may be given with MMR.
No later boosters of the conjugate are advised in subsequent years.

viva.q: How is the polysaccharide typhoid vaccine given?
viva.a: 0.5 mL intramuscular after 2 years of age, repeated every 3 years.

viva.q: How does the conjugate vaccine differ?
viva.a: One dose from 6 months onward, with MMR if due, and no later boosters.

unsure: Book prints TCV 25 mg, which reads like a unit slip for micrograms, so the figure was left out.

items.summary: Live and killed vaccines against Japanese encephalitis with schedules by product type.

blocks.title: Strain and effect
bullets: A cell culture live vaccine raised from the stable weakened SA-14-14-2 strain.
One dose protects about 99 percent.

blocks.title: Schedules by type
bullets: Live weakened vaccine: a single 0.5 mL dose under the skin at 8 months or older.
Live recombinant vaccine: a single dose at 9 months or older.
Killed vero cell vaccine: two doses 4 weeks apart, starting at 6 months or older in endemic areas.

viva.q: What strain is the live JE vaccine made from?
viva.a: The stable neuroattenuated SA-14-14-2 strain grown in cell culture.

viva.q: How many doses does each JE type need?
viva.a: One dose for either live type, two doses 4 weeks apart for the killed vero cell type.

items.summary: Live oral vaccines against infantile diarrhoea with strict age limits for the course.

blocks.title: Products and doses
bullets: Three live oral products are in use.
Rotarix: 2 mL by mouth in two doses 4 weeks apart.
Rotateq: 3 mL by mouth in three doses 4 weeks apart, or at 2, 4 and 6 months of age.
Rotavac: three oral doses with at least 4 weeks between doses.

blocks.title: Age limits and bar
bullets: Start the first dose before 16 weeks of age and finish the course by 32 weeks.
Prior intussusception bars the vaccine absolutely.

viva.q: How is Rotarix given?
viva.a: 2 mL oral in two doses 4 weeks apart, starting before 16 weeks.

viva.q: By when must the course finish?
viva.a: By 32 weeks of age, with the first dose before 16 weeks.

viva.q: When is rotavirus vaccine absolutely barred?
viva.a: After a past episode of intussusception.

items.summary: Live chickenpox vaccine in two doses, preferably timed with MMR.

blocks.title: Dose and timing
bullets: A live weakened vaccine raised from the Oka strain.
After 1 year of age, give 0.5 mL under the skin in two doses 8 to 12 weeks apart.
Prefer to give it with MMR at or after 15 months.

blocks.title: Handling
bullets: Shield it from light and inject within 30 minutes of mixing.
Mix with sterile water.

viva.q: What is the varicella schedule?
viva.a: 0.5 mL subcutaneous after 1 year, two doses 8 to 12 weeks apart, preferably with MMR from 15 months.

viva.q: How do you handle the mixed vaccine?
viva.a: Protect it from light and use within 30 minutes of reconstitution.

items.summary: Killed hepatitis A vaccine in two deltoid doses for children above 1 year.

blocks.title: Dose and schedule
bullets: A killed virus vaccine carried on aluminium hydroxide adjuvant.
After 1 year of age, give 0.5 mL into the deltoid in two doses 6 to 12 months apart.

blocks.title: Prior infection
bullets: No vaccine is needed after past hepatitis A illness.

viva.q: What is the hepatitis A schedule?
viva.a: 0.5 mL intramuscular at the deltoid after 1 year, two doses 6 to 12 months apart.

viva.q: Does a child with past hepatitis A need it?
viva.a: No. Past infection removes the need for vaccination.

items.summary: Recombinant vaccines against cervical cancer given to girls before sexual activity.

blocks.title: Products
bullets: Quadrivalent Gardasil covers types 6, 11, 16 and 18, while bivalent Cervarix covers 16 and 18.
Both are built by recombinant DNA as non infectious virus like particles.

blocks.title: Whom and how many
bullets: Target girls 9 to 14 years old, before sexual activity, to prevent cervical cancer.
Two doses 6 months apart when the first comes before 15 years of age.
Three doses at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months from 15 years up, or when immunocompromised or HIV infected at any younger age regardless of treatment.

blocks.title: Pregnancy and dose
bullets: Safety data in pregnancy are limited, so avoid vaccinating pregnant women.
Give 0.5 mL into the deltoid.

viva.q: Who should receive HPV vaccine?
viva.a: Girls 9 to 14 years old, before becoming sexually active, to prevent cervical cancer.

viva.q: When is the 3 dose schedule used?
viva.a: From 15 years up, or in immunocompromised and HIV infected children, at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months.

viva.q: Can you vaccinate a pregnant woman?
viva.a: No. Safety data are limited, so HPV vaccination in pregnancy is avoided.

items.summary: Tissue culture rabies vaccines for bite treatment and prevention, with antibody cover for severe bites.

blocks.title: Products
bullets: Killed tissue culture vaccines: chick embryo cell Rabipur, human diploid cell Rabivax, and vero cell Verorab.

blocks.title: Bite schedule
bullets: After exposure, give 1 mL into muscle in five doses on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28.

blocks.title: Preventive schedule
bullets: For prevention, give 1 mL into muscle in three doses on days 0, 7 and 28.

blocks.title: Antibodies with the vaccine
bullets: Monoclonal antibody may replace immunoglobulin for category III bites.
Mix with sterile water and use within 6 hours of mixing.
Immunoglobulin dosing is 20 units per kg for human and 40 for equine product.
Rabisheild at 40 IU per mL is licensed since 2017 at 3.33 IU per kg with the first vaccine dose.

viva.q: What is the post bite rabies schedule?
viva.a: 1 mL intramuscular in five doses on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28.

viva.q: What is the preventive schedule?
viva.a: 1 mL intramuscular in three doses on days 0, 7 and 28.

viva.q: What antibody cover goes with the vaccine in category III bites?
viva.a: Rabies immunoglobulin or monoclonal antibody such as Rabisheild at 3.33 IU per kg.

items.summary: Yearly killed influenza vaccine for all young children from 6 months of age.

blocks.title: Whom and when
bullets: Killed trivalent or quadrivalent vaccine is advised yearly for all children below 5 years from 6 months.
Give it 2 to 4 weeks before the influenza season.

blocks.title: Dose
bullets: Give 0.5 mL into muscle in two doses 4 weeks apart, with a yearly booster.

viva.q: Which children need influenza vaccine?
viva.a: All children below 5 years from 6 months of age, every year.

viva.q: What is the dosing pattern?
viva.a: 0.5 mL intramuscular in two doses 4 weeks apart, then a booster each year.

items.summary: The government schedule of vaccines by age from birth through pregnancy, with the vitamin A cycle.

blocks.title: How to read it
blocks.text: Find the age on the left and read across for every vaccine due. Birth doses assume an institutional delivery, and vitamin A runs on its own six monthly cycle.

head: Age
Vaccines due
rows: BCG, OPV zero dose, hepatitis B first dose
Pentavalent first dose, rotavirus first dose, PCV first dose, fractional IPV first dose, bivalent OPV first dose, plus BCG if missed at birth
Pentavalent second dose, rotavirus second dose, bivalent OPV second dose, plus BCG if missed at birth
Pentavalent third dose, rotavirus third dose, PCV second dose, fractional IPV second dose, bivalent OPV third dose, plus BCG if missed at birth
MR first dose, JE first dose, vitamin A 1 Lac IU
DTwP booster 1, OPV booster, MR second dose, JE second dose, PCV booster
TT first dose early in pregnancy, TT second dose one month later, TT booster if vaccinated in past 3 years
9 total doses from 9 months every 6 months to 5 years, 2 Lac IU after 1 year

viva.q: Which vaccines are due at birth?
viva.a: BCG, OPV zero dose and hepatitis B first dose for institutional deliveries.

viva.q: What is due at 9 to 12 months?
viva.a: MR first dose, JE first dose, and vitamin A 1 Lac IU.

viva.q: What TT does a pregnant woman need?
viva.a: Two doses a month apart starting early in pregnancy, or one booster if vaccinated in the past 3 years.

items.summary: The academy timetable of routine childhood vaccines from birth to late adolescence, with vitamin A dosing.

blocks.title: How to read it
blocks.text: Read down the age column and across for each vaccine due at that visit. Pentavalent rows stand for diphtheria, pertussis, hepatitis B and Hib antigens given together.

head: Age
Vaccines due
rows: BCG, OPV zero dose, hepatitis B first dose
DTwP or DTaP first dose, IPV first dose, hepatitis B second dose, Hib first dose, rotavirus first dose, PCV first dose
DTwP or DTaP second dose, IPV second dose, Hib second dose, rotavirus second dose, PCV second dose
DTwP or DTaP third dose, IPV third dose, Hib third dose, rotavirus third dose, PCV third dose
OPV first dose, influenza first dose, typhoid conjugate
OPV second dose, MMR first dose, typhoid, influenza second dose
MMR second dose, PCV booster, chickenpox first dose
DTwP or DTaP booster 1, IPV booster 1, Hib booster 1, hepatitis A second dose
DTwP or DTaP booster 2, OPV third dose, MMR third dose, chickenpox second dose, typhoid

blocks.title: Vitamin A doses
blocks.text: Below 6 months give 50,000 IU, from 6 months to 1 year give 1 Lac IU, and above 1 year give 2 Lac IU, all by mouth.

viva.q: What is due at 6 weeks in the IAP timetable?
viva.a: DTwP or DTaP, IPV, hepatitis B, Hib, rotavirus and PCV first doses.

viva.q: What is due at 15 months?
viva.a: MMR second dose, PCV booster and chickenpox first dose.

viva.q: What is advised at 9 to 14 years?
viva.a: Tdap with the first two HPV doses.

items.summary: Extra vaccines advised under special circumstances and the children who qualify for them.

blocks.title: Extra vaccines
bullets: Influenza vaccine.
Meningococcal vaccine.
Japanese encephalitis vaccine.
Cholera vaccine.
Rabies vaccine.
Yellow fever vaccine.
23 valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine.

blocks.title: Who counts as high risk
bullets: Immune deficiency from birth or later, including HIV infection.
Long standing heart, lung, blood, kidney including nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, and diabetes.
Asthma treated with prolonged high dose oral steroids.
Long term steroids, salicylates, immune suppressing or radiation treatment.
Diabetes, spinal fluid leak, cochlear implant, and cancers.
Absent or weak spleen function.
Outbreak settings.
Laboratory and health care workers.
Travellers.

viva.q: Name three vaccines kept for special circumstances.
viva.a: Meningococcal, yellow fever and cholera vaccines, besides influenza, JE, rabies and PPSV 23.

viva.q: Which chronic conditions place a child in the high risk group?
viva.a: Heart, lung, kidney, liver and blood disorders with diabetes, and asthma on prolonged high dose steroids.

viva.q: Does a child without a spleen need extra vaccines?
viva.a: Yes. Absent or weak spleen function places the child in the high risk group.

items.summary: Single preparations that join two or more immunising parts so one shot covers several diseases.

blocks.title: What it means
blocks.text: Two or more separate immunising parts are physically joined into one preparation, so a single shot protects against several diseases at once.

blocks.title: Examples in the book
bullets: DTPw with Hib.
DTPw with hepatitis B.
DTPw with Hib and hepatitis B.
Hepatitis A with hepatitis B.
MMR.
DPwT.
DTPw with IPV, Hib and hepatitis B.

viva.q: What is a combination vaccine?
viva.a: Two or more separate immunising parts joined in one preparation, so one shot covers several diseases.

viva.q: Give two examples.
viva.a: DTPw with Hib, and DTPw with hepatitis B, besides MMR and larger combinations.
